Labor supported the National Housing Finance and Investment Corporation Amendment Bill 2019, which creates a First Home Loan Deposit Scheme allowing eligible singles earning under $125,000 or couples under $200,000 to purchase a home with a 5% deposit, capped at 10,000 purchases per year. Labor moved a second reading amendment noting that under the government home ownership fell to its lowest level since the 1960s, mortgage arrears reached their highest since the global financial crisis, over 1 million low-income households were in housing stress, and homelessness exceeded 116,000.

The member for Dunkley supported the National Housing Finance and Investment Corporation Amendment Bill 2019 and its second reading amendment, citing that 26% of homeless Victorians are under 25 and that 4,060 young people sought help in the Bayside Peninsula area in 2016–17. She called for bipartisan funding to build two supported crisis accommodation facilities near Frankston and Rosebud and a youth foyer linked to education providers.

The National Housing Finance and Investment Corporation Amendment Bill 2019 expands the NHFIC to help 10,000 first home buyers per year with a 5% deposit and adds a research function on housing supply and demand. The speaker also highlighted record infrastructure investments in Western Sydney, including the Western Sydney International Airport and North South Rail, and the importance of affordable housing for key workers, domestic violence survivors, and older people.

The speech supported the National Housing Finance and Investment Corporation Amendment Bill 2019, which establishes a First Home Loan Deposit Scheme providing 10,000 guarantees per year on loans with deposits between 5% and 20%, limited to incomes under $125,000 for singles and $200,000 for couples. It also raised concerns about the scheme's limited scale, unclear regional pricing caps and boundaries, and the distribution of guarantees across states, urging expansion and additional housing measures.

The National Housing Finance and Investment Corporation Amendment Bill 2019 enables the NHFIC to provide 10,000 guarantees per year for first home buyers and establish a research function on housing affordability, with the First Home Loan Deposit Scheme commencing 1 January 2020 and an investment mandate to be released for public consultation.

The Criminal Code Amendment (Agricultural Protection) Bill 2019 introduces new offences for using a carriage service to incite trespass, property damage, destruction or theft on agricultural land, with penalties of up to 12 months imprisonment for inciting trespass and up to five years for inciting damage or theft. The bill includes exemptions for journalists and whistleblowers, and builds on earlier action to prescribe the Aussie Farms website under the Privacy Act, exposing it to potential penalties of up to $2.1 million.

Labor argued the bill may be unnecessary due to existing state and territory laws already criminalising trespass, property damage and theft, and raised concerns it could infringe on democratic rights, whistleblower protections, journalism, native title access and legitimate industrial action. Labor will not oppose the bill in the House but will await the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee's report before announcing a final position.

The Criminal Code Amendment (Agricultural Protection) Bill 2019 is a necessary response to online incitement of trespass and property offences against farmers, and the bill was commended to the House.

The speaker moved the second reading of the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Police Powers at Airports) Bill, which expands police powers to conduct identity checks and issue move-on directions at major airports based on reasonable suspicion of serious offences or to safeguard public order, creates new offences with fines up to $4,200, and incorporates recommendations from parliamentary committees.

The speaker supported the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Police Powers at Airports) Bill 2019, noting that the revised version implements six of eight bipartisan recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, including requiring the Australian Federal Police to record and publicly report annually on the use of the new powers, and clarifying that the powers cannot be used to disrupt peaceful assembly or protest.

The government argued the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Police Powers at Airports) Bill 2019 gives police broader powers to conduct identity checks and issue move-on directions for up to 24 hours at major airports to counter terrorism and organised crime, citing attacks in Brussels (2016), Istanbul (2016), Paris Orly (2017) and a foiled Sydney-to-Abu Dhabi plot (2017). The bill includes safeguards preventing use against peaceful protests and ensuring judicial review rights.

The speaker supported a Senate amendment to insert a four-year sunset clause and a statutory review into the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Police Powers at Airports) Bill 2019, requiring the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security to review the provisions in three years. The amendment, moved by Senator Patrick, would force Parliament to decide whether to re-endorse, amend, or let the new coercive powers expire.

The speaker moved a motion to change committee memberships, discharging Senator Urquhart and appointing Senator Gallacher to the National Disability Insurance Scheme Joint Standing Committee, and appointing substitute members for several other committees including Wright, Milne, and Ludlam.

The speaker presented the Environment Legislation Amendment Bill 2013 to provide legal certainty for past conservation decisions under the EPBC Act and triple criminal and civil penalties for poaching and illegal trade of turtles and dugong. The Infrastructure Australia Amendment Bill 2013 was introduced to restructure the agency as an independent authority, conduct five-yearly audits, develop a 15-year infrastructure plan, and review all Commonwealth-funded projects over $100 million. The Migration Amendment (Regaining Control Over Australia’s Protection Obligations) Bill 2013 removes the complementary protection criterion from the Migration Act, reverting to an administrative process for assessing non-refoulement obligations under the CAT and ICCPR, while maintaining those obligations.
Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Bill 2013

The coalition opposed the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Bill 2013, arguing it was being rushed through parliament without the necessary detail or consultation, despite the Auditor-General and other officials recommending more time. The speaker supported the bill’s principles but opposed its passage, warning that key rules had not been drafted and that haste risked mismanagement of over $350 billion in revenue and $640 billion in liabilities.
